lessons.title: Uncertain outcomes at work
objectives: Stay effective during reorganisations and waiting.
teach: When outcomes are unknown, focus on what you control: quality of work, relationships, information gathering, and preparation for options.
Limit information-checking to set times to avoid rumination.
Name the uncertainty with colleagues without spreading catastrophes.

Uncertainty at work is often shared. Talking with colleagues can help, as long as conversations stay on facts and options rather than amplifying worst cases. A useful question for a group is: "What do we actually know, and what can we prepare for either way?"

Waiting periods can also be used. Some people use them to strengthen skills or relationships that would help in any outcome. This turns a passive, anxious wait into a period of preparation, without pretending to know what will happen.
lessons.example: During a merger, Imran lists controllables: deliver the current project well, keep good working relationships, update his CV, and ask HR one clear question. He checks news at 9am and 5pm only. He still feels anxious, but less stuck.
practicePrompts: List three controllables in a current uncertainty.
lessons.apply: Write "What we know / What we can prepare" for one uncertainty at work.
lessons.reflect: What can you control this month?

lessons.title: Recovery after a hard meeting
teach: After a difficult meeting: reset the body (walk, breathe), note facts and actions while fresh, then switch attention deliberately to the next task.
Avoid replaying the meeting abstractly; if you review, do it concretely with a next step.
Self-distanced reflection can help process it.

Recovery is not the same as forgetting. The aim is to take what is useful from the meeting (actions, lessons) and then return attention to the rest of your day. If the meeting keeps returning, schedule a short, concrete review rather than fighting the thought.

Notice what you say about the meeting to others. A brief, factual account to a trusted colleague can help you process it. Retelling the most painful moments many times to different people tends to keep it alive. If you need to talk it through, choose one person and one conversation.
lessons.example: After a hard call, Priya walks for five minutes, writes three lines (what was agreed, what she will do, by when), and then says to herself, "Next task: the budget sheet." In the evening she reflects once, in third person, for five minutes.
practicePrompts: Write a three-step recovery routine.
lessons.apply: After your next tense meeting, use the four-step routine and note how long it took.
lessons.reflect: What is your recovery routine?

lessons.title: Disagreeing with seniors
teach: Disagreeing with someone senior can trigger fear. Prepare: shared goal, specific concern, evidence, proposal.
"I share the goal of X. I'm concerned Y because Z. Could we try W?"
Accept that they may still decide differently.

When power is unequal. Disagreeing with someone who controls your pay, workload or reputation carries more risk than disagreeing with a peer. That risk is real, not a sign of weakness. It changes the tactics, not the right to raise concerns: put the issue in terms of shared goals, bring evidence, offer options, and choose a private setting. Keep a short written record of important agreements. If the issue involves mistreatment, use formal routes such as HR rather than handling it alone.

When incentives differ. People may disagree because they are measured on different things: sales wants speed, compliance wants caution. Naming the different incentives ("I think we are both right about what we are each responsible for") can move the conversation from blame to trade-offs. Example: your director wants a launch date you think is unsafe. Instead of "That is impossible", you say: "I want us to hit the date too. Here are two risks, and two options: drop feature B, or move a week. Which would you prefer?"

Fear of disagreeing upward is common and understandable: the other person has more power. Preparing your script in advance lowers the load in the moment. It also helps to choose the setting: a private conversation or a written note is often easier than a large meeting.

Accept that you may not change the decision. Disagreeing well means your concern is on record and has been considered. If the decision stands and it is not an ethical or safety issue, committing to it while keeping your reservation noted is a professional choice, not a defeat.
lessons.example: "I share the goal of launching this quarter. I am concerned that skipping user testing risks a costly fix later, because the last two launches needed patches. Could we test with five users this week?" The director still decides to skip; she documents her concern and supports the launch.
practicePrompts: Write a disagreement script for a current issue.
lessons.apply: Draft a three-sentence upward disagreement for a real or past situation.
lessons.reflect: What disagreement are you holding back?

lessons.title: Professional drills
teach: Complete three professional-context gym scenarios across categories.
Apply fact versus interpretation first.

Professional situations add role obligations: confidentiality, clients, team commitments, and the reputation of your organisation. These shape which responses are available, but they rarely require you to pretend you feel nothing. The question is not only "what do I feel and want?" but also "what does my role require here, and how can I meet it while being honest about my concerns?"

These drills mix all the professional skills. Expect some scenarios to have no perfect answer. The aim is to choose a response you could defend later: one that respects your role, the other person, and your own limits. Use the feedback to understand trade-offs rather than to memorise answers, since real situations will differ in details.
lessons.example: Gym run: credit taken (private conversation plus written follow-up), new role with unclear expectations (drafted role summary), reorganisation rumours (controllables, limited checking). Each started with separating facts from interpretations.
practicePrompts: Complete three professional scenarios.
lessons.apply: Complete the professional scenarios in the gym that you have not tried yet.
lessons.reflect: Which professional skill is strongest now?

lessons.title: Professional composure checkpoint
teach: Phase checkpoint. 80% or more marks mastery (design choice). This checkpoint covers phase 8, professional composure: stay effective under pressure, demands and uncertainty at work.

Questions are drawn from a pool of the phase's items, with alternatives, so a retake shows different questions where possible. Up to two questions come from earlier phases to keep older skills active. If you miss questions, the results screen lists the lessons to revisit.
practicePrompts: Answer from memory.
lessons.apply: Pick the skill from this phase you found hardest and use it once in a real situation this week, then record it in the Journal.
lessons.reflect: What does composure look like for you now?

lessons.title: Mapping your patterns
teach: Look at your journal: which situations recur, which interpretations, which urges, which outcomes? The Progress page shows your most frequent emotions and triggers.
Describe patterns, not causes. "I tend to get defensive when feedback is public" is a pattern. "Because of my childhood" is a causal claim this data cannot support.
Patterns point to where if-then plans help most.

Why habits persist. Many unhelpful responses persist because they bring quick relief. Avoiding an email lowers anxiety for a moment. Snapping at someone releases tension. Checking your phone ends boredom. The relief rewards the response, so it becomes more likely next time, even when the long-term cost is high. Looking at the short-term pay-off is not blame. It explains why willpower alone often does not change the pattern.

Patterns are not causes. A journal can show that you often feel irritated on Monday evenings after meetings with one colleague. That is an observed pattern. "My colleague makes me angry because of my childhood" is a causal hypothesis, and your notes cannot confirm it. Keep patterns descriptive, and treat explanations as hypotheses to test. Example: you notice that you postpone difficult calls until late afternoon. The pattern is clear. A hypothesis you can test is "I put calls off because the first minute feels worst", and a small change will show whether it holds.

Patterns appear when you look across several entries rather than one. Look for repeats in triggers (time of day, people, tasks), emotions, urges and outcomes. Be careful about causes: a pattern shows what tends to happen together, not why. "I often feel irritable after long meetings" is a pattern; "because I am an introvert" is an explanation you have not tested.
lessons.example: Journal review: frustration appears in 9 of 14 entries; 7 of those follow meetings where decisions changed late. Pattern: "I get frustrated when plans change without notice." Not: "I am an angry person because of my upbringing." The plan: ask for decision deadlines.
practicePrompts: Open Progress and review your top triggers.
Write one pattern statement.
lessons.apply: Look at your Progress page and journal, and write one pattern and one small experiment to test it.
lessons.reflect: What pattern stands out?

lessons.title: When to seek more support
teach: This app is training, not therapy or crisis support. If emotions are persistently overwhelming, if you feel unsafe, or if daily functioning is affected, talking to a qualified professional is a sensible step.
In India: in an emergency, dial 112. For free mental-health support, Tele-MANAS answers on 14416 or 1-800-891-4416. Both are government services.

Self-guided training has limits. Consider professional support if emotions often feel unmanageable, if they interfere with work, sleep or relationships for weeks, if you are using alcohol or other substances to cope, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself or others. Seeking help is a skill, not a failure: you can start with a GP, a counsellor, or a helpline, and you do not need to be in crisis to call.
lessons.example: Over two months, Anil notices he cannot sleep, has stopped seeing friends, and the techniques feel out of reach. He books an appointment with a counsellor. Using the lab did not fail; it helped him notice the need for more support.
practicePrompts: Note one person and one professional option you could contact.
lessons.apply: Write down one person or service you would contact if things became too much.
lessons.reflect: Who is in your support network?

lessons.title: Maintenance plan
teach: Skills fade without use. Spaced reviews in this app bring back items at 2, 7 and 21 days after mastery.
Keep if-then plans for your top three triggers.

Notice which skills you actually use. After a few weeks, most people rely on two or three. That is fine. Use the gym to keep one less familiar skill in reach, so you are not left with only one tool when a new kind of situation arrives.

Expect gaps. Most people miss practice weeks during holidays, illness or busy periods. A maintenance plan should make restarting easy: one check-in, one review session. Starting again is part of the plan, not a failure of it.

A sustainable plan is small: for example, two check-ins a week, one gym scenario a week, and whatever reviews the app shows as due. Put it on a cue you already have. Decide now what restarting looks like after a gap, so that missing a week does not become stopping altogether.
lessons.example: Maintenance plan: check-in on Monday and Thursday after lunch; one gym scenario on Saturday morning; reviews when the badge shows any due; keep three if-then plans for meetings, late messages and criticism.
practicePrompts: Write your maintenance plan in the Journal.
lessons.apply: Write your maintenance plan as two or three if-then plans in the Journal.
lessons.reflect: What maintenance will you keep?

lessons.title: Integration drill
objectives: Use the full chain on a real event.
teach: Take a real recent event and run the full chain: facts, interpretations, emotions with intensity, urge, strategy chosen, outcome, lesson.
Then write one if-then plan for next time.

Small experiments. Once you have a hypothesis about a pattern, test it with a small, safe, time-limited change. Write the prediction first ("If I make the hard call at 10 am, I predict it will feel at least as bad as at 4 pm"). Do it for a week. Then compare what happened with what you predicted. Keep the change small enough that you can actually run it, and observable enough that you can tell what happened.

Revising. If the result does not support your hypothesis, that is useful information, not a failure. Revise the hypothesis or try a different change. If it is supported, keep the change and look for the next small step. Example: you suspect that you ruminate less on evenings when you walk after work. You walk on three evenings and not on three others, and note your rumination each night from 0 to 10. If the numbers are similar, the walk may not be the key factor, and you can test something else, such as stopping work email at 7 pm.

The integration drill combines every skill from the programme in one pass. It will feel slower than real life at first. With repetition, many steps become quick and partly automatic, which is the point of practising them deliberately now.

When you apply the full chain to a real event, write it down afterwards. Notice which links came naturally and which you had to reach for. The ones you had to reach for are your next focus for practice. Over time, the chain often becomes shorter and quicker, because several steps happen together.
lessons.example: Event: a client complaint. Facts: email at 4pm listing two issues. Interpretation: "I will lose this client." Emotions: anxiety 7, embarrassment 4. Urge: defend. Strategy: breathe, separate facts, call the client. Outcome: issues fixed. Lesson: call earlier. Plan: "If a complaint arrives, then I call within the hour."
practicePrompts: Complete a full Journal reflection with all fields.
lessons.apply: Apply the full chain to one real event this week and record it as a full reflection.
lessons.reflect: What did the full chain reveal?

lessons.title: Final checkpoint
teach: Final checkpoint. Then take the post-programme assessment from Progress. 80% threshold is a design choice. This checkpoint covers phase 9, patterns and maintenance: map recurring patterns and build a sustainable practice.

Questions are drawn from a pool of the phase's items, with alternatives, so a retake shows different questions where possible. Up to two questions come from earlier phases to keep older skills active. If you miss questions, the results screen lists the lessons to revisit.
practicePrompts: Answer from memory.
lessons.apply: Pick the skill from this phase you found hardest and use it once in a real situation this week, then record it in the Journal.
lessons.reflect: What will you carry forward?

concepts.label: Given an everyday episode, you can say what the emotion was signalling and show that feeling it did not oblige a particular action.
You can break an episode into situation, interpretation, body, urge, action and outcome, in the right order.
You can tell habitual suppression apart from a deliberate, time-limited choice to hold back, and explain the cost of the habit.
You can explain why retrieval and spacing are used here, and why self-ratings and check scores are kept separate.
Demonstrate the foundations.
You can replace a vague word such as "stressed" with a more precise emotion word that fits the situation.
You can name a feeling in words during an episode and describe what that naming is and is not expected to do.
You can identify two or more emotions present at once, including one that may be hidden by another.
You can run a 30-second check-in: emotion, intensity, and one body signal.
Demonstrate precise noticing and naming.
You can locate and describe bodily signals of an emotion without judging them.
You can notice an urge, name it, and choose whether and when to act on it.
You can explain why venting tends to keep anger going and pick a lower-arousal alternative.
You can carry out a short breathing or grounding reset and say when it fits and when it does not.
Demonstrate body and impulse skills.
You can sort statements about an event into camera facts and interpretations.
You can produce at least three plausible readings of an ambiguous event.
You can spot mind-reading, catastrophising and all-or-nothing thinking without treating every negative thought as a distortion.
You can weigh evidence for and against an interpretation and state what remains uncertain.
Retrieve interpretation skills.
You can describe an event from a self-distanced perspective.
You can use temporal distance to put a current upset in proportion.
You can explain acceptance as allowing a feeling while acting on what matters, not as giving up.
You can produce a fast, fair reappraisal that is not just positive thinking.
Demonstrate interpretation skills (weeks 4-5).
You can name the main strategy families and judge when expressing an emotion fits.
You can match a strategy to emotional intensity.
You can turn a stressor into one concrete next step.
You can write a specific if-then plan for a predictable trigger.
Demonstrate strategy matching.
You can tell rumination from reflection using the "is there a next step?" test.
You can set up and run a worry window.
You can act while uncertain and tell protective avoidance from restrictive avoidance.
You can review a setback for controllable and uncontrollable parts and pick one lesson.
Demonstrate these skills.
You can hear criticism, ask one clarifying question, and delay your evaluation.
You can sort feedback into accurate, partly accurate and inaccurate parts.
You can respond to provocation without escalating, choosing to respond, delay, disengage or set a boundary.
You can plan a difficult conversation: goal, opening line and a fallback.
Retrieve criticism skills.
You can state a boundary assertively, and tell assertive from aggressive and passive responses.
You can make a specific repair after a conflict.
You can validate another person's feeling without having to agree.
You can choose a proportionate response in a conflict scenario and explain its trade-off.
Demonstrate weeks 8-9 skills.
You can stay effective at work while feeling strong emotion, without going cold.
You can answer an excessive demand with options instead of a flat yes or no.
You can use a pressure routine: pause, state the trade-off, decide, set a review point.
You can apply the pressure routine to unfamiliar work scenarios.
Retrieve composure skills.
You can stay effective during workplace uncertainty by separating controllables from rumours.
You can reset after a difficult meeting with a short recovery routine.
You can disagree upward, adapting tactics for unequal power and different incentives.
You can combine composure skills in mixed professional scenarios.
Demonstrate weeks 10-11.
You can describe a recurring pattern without claiming its cause, and explain the role of short-term relief.
You can recognise signs that self-training is not enough and further support is worth seeking.
You can write a realistic maintenance plan.
You can design a small behavioural experiment and revise your hypothesis from the result.
Demonstrate integration.
